rabat.s: Rabat is a city on the Atlantic coast of Morocco, now the country's capital. Under the Almohad Caliphate it was developed as a fortified military base.

rabih-az-zubayr.s: Rabih az-Zubayr was a Sudanese warlord and slave trader who built a powerful state in the Lake Chad region in the late nineteenth century. He conquered Bornu in 1893 and threatened Wadai.

rabihs-conquest-of-bornu.s: Rabih's conquest of Bornu was the seizure of the kingdom of Bornu, the successor of the Kanem-Bornu Empire, by the Sudanese warlord Rabih az-Zubayr in 1893. It overthrew the old ruling order west of Lake Chad.

racial-segregation.s: Racial segregation is the enforced separation of people of different races in housing, public life and rights. The Italian Empire codified racial segregation in its African colonies through a series of laws, particularly after the conquest of Ethiopia.

raden-wijaya.s: Raden Wijaya was the founder and first ruler of the Majapahit Empire in eastern Java, reigning from 1293 to 1309 CE. He used a Mongol expedition sent by Kublai Khan of the Yuan Dynasty to defeat his rivals, then turned against the Mongol forces and drove them out.

raffia-cloth.s: Raffia cloth is a textile woven from the fibres of the raffia palm, produced in Central Africa. In the Kingdom of Kongo it was a valuable good and also served as a form of currency.

ragamuffin-war.s: The Ragamuffin War, or Farroupilha, was a republican and separatist revolt in the southern Brazilian province of Rio Grande do Sul, lasting from 1835 to 1845. It was the longest of the provincial rebellions that shook the Brazilian Empire during and after the Regency period.

raigad.s: Raigad is a hill fort in the Western Ghats of Maharashtra, India. It was one of the strategic forts controlled by Shivaji and became his capital.

rajapur.s: Rajapur is a port town on the Konkan coast of Maharashtra, western India. Under the Maratha Empire it was one of the ports, alongside Dabhol, through which maritime trade linked the Deccan to the Arabian Sea.

rajendra-chola-i.s: Rajendra Chola I was an emperor of the Chola dynasty of southern India in the early eleventh century. In 1025 he launched a major naval expedition against the Srivijaya Empire, raiding its ports.

rajgad.s: Rajgad is a hill fort in the Sahyadri range near Pune in Maharashtra. It was one of the key forts secured by Shivaji in building his power in the Western Ghats.

rajputs.s: The Rajputs are a group of warrior clans of northern and western India, many of whom ruled kingdoms in Rajasthan and neighbouring regions. They resisted the Delhi Sultanate and the early Mughal Empire, as at the Battle of Khanwa against Babur in 1527, but many later became…

ramadan.s: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, observed by Muslims as a month of fasting, prayer and reflection. According to the site's Almohad Caliphate profile, it was towards the end of Ramadan in 1121 that Ibn Tumart proclaimed himself the Mahdi.

ramesses-ii.s: Ramesses II was a pharaoh of the Nineteenth Dynasty of the Egyptian New Kingdom, who reigned for much of the thirteenth century BCE. He fought the Hittite king Muwatalli II at the Battle of Kadesh in 1274 BCE and later concluded a peace treaty with the Hittite Empire.

ramesses-iii.s: Ramesses III was a pharaoh of the Twentieth Dynasty of the Egyptian New Kingdom. He defeated land and sea invasions by the Sea Peoples around 1177 BCE, preserving Egypt during the Late Bronze Age collapse.

ramesses-xi.s: Ramesses XI was the last pharaoh of the Twentieth Dynasty and of the Egyptian New Kingdom. During his reign real power passed to the high priests of Amun in Thebes and to military commanders.

rampjaar.s: The Rampjaar, or disaster year, was 1672 in the history of the Dutch Republic. France under Louis XIV invaded with a vast army while England attacked by sea, and the republic was nearly overrun.

rangaku.s: Rangaku, meaning Dutch learning, was the body of European scientific and technical knowledge studied in Japan through the Dutch trading post at Dejima. During the Tokugawa Shogunate's period of restricted foreign contact, Japanese scholars translated and analysed European…

ranjit-singh.s: Ranjit Singh was the founder and Maharaja of the Sikh Empire, who lived from 1780 to 1839. Born into the Sukerchakia Misl, he seized Lahore in 1799 and united the Sikh confederacies of the Punjab under his rule.

ras.s: Ras, meaning head, was one of the highest noble and military titles in the Ethiopian Empire, below that of the negus. It was held by powerful regional lords and governors.

rashid-al-din-hamadani.s: Rashid al-Din Hamadani was a Persian physician, statesman and historian who served as vizier of the Ilkhanate. He carried out the extensive reforms of Ghazan Khan and wrote the Jami al-Tawarikh, a universal history of Eurasia.

rashidun-caliphate.s: The Rashidun Caliphate was the first Islamic caliphate, ruled by the four rightly guided caliphs Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali from the death of the Prophet Muhammad in 632 CE until 661 CE. It reunified Arabia in the Ridda Wars and conquered the Sasanian Empire and the…

rastafari.s: Rastafari is a religious and cultural movement that emerged in Jamaica in the 1930s. It regards Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia as a messianic figure.

ravi.s: The Ravi is one of the five rivers of the Punjab, flowing from the Himalayas through India and Pakistan, with Lahore on its banks. With the Jhelum, Chenab, Beas and Sutlej, it sustained intensive cultivation of wheat, cotton and sugarcane.

rayy.s: Rayy was an ancient city in northern Iran, near modern Tehran, and a major centre on the Silk Road. Under the Seljuk Empire it was one of the cities, alongside Nishapur and Isfahan, from which sultans drew substantial revenue by taxing caravan traffic.

reconquista.s: The Reconquista refers to the centuries-long series of campaigns by Christian kingdoms of the Iberian Peninsula to conquer the territories ruled by Muslims, completed with the fall of Granada in 1492. The Almoravid Empire and the Almohad Caliphate intervened in al-Andalus to…

recopilacion-de-leyes-de-los-reinos-de-l.n: Recopilación de Leyes de los Reinos de las Indias
recopilacion-de-leyes-de-los-reinos-de-l.s: The Recopilación de Leyes de los Reinos de las Indias was a comprehensive compilation of the laws governing Spain's American territories, published in 1680. It was produced under the Council of the Indies, which governed the colonies from Madrid.

red-sea.s: The Red Sea is a narrow arm of the Indian Ocean between north-east Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, connected to the Mediterranean by the Suez isthmus. It has long been a major trade route between the Mediterranean, Arabia, India and East Africa.

red-turban-rebellion.s: The Red Turban Rebellion was a series of uprisings against Mongol rule in China, beginning in 1351 under the influence of White Lotus millenarian beliefs and lasting to 1368. It spread across central China and produced competing warlords.

regency-period-brazil.s: The Regency period was the era from 1831 to 1840 when Brazil was governed by regents on behalf of the young Pedro II after his father's abdication. It was marked by serial provincial rebellions, including the Cabanagem and the Ragamuffin War.

regional-autonomy-and-warlordism.s: Regional autonomy and warlordism are a recurring cause of imperial decline, as provincial governors, generals or local lords accumulate independent military and fiscal power and cease to obey the centre. The process fragments the state and often leads to civil war.

reichsrat.s: The Reichsrat was the parliament of the Austrian half of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, sitting in Vienna. Under the 1867 Compromise it governed the Austrian lands, while the Hungarian Diet in Budapest governed the Hungarian half.

reichstag.s: The Reichstag was the national parliament of the German Empire, elected by universal male suffrage. It voted on legislation and the budget but could not appoint or remove ministers, who were responsible to the Kaiser alone.

reinsurance-treaty.s: The Reinsurance Treaty was a secret agreement between the German Empire and Russia, concluded by Bismarck in 1887, in which each promised neutrality in most wars involving the other. After Bismarck's dismissal it was allowed to lapse in 1890.

reliance-on-mercenaries.s: Reliance on mercenaries is a recurring structural feature of empires that hire foreign or professional soldiers instead of relying on citizen or subject levies. Mercenaries can provide skilled forces quickly but are costly and may mutiny or change sides when pay fails.

religious-legitimacy.s: Religious legitimacy is a recurring source of imperial strength, as rulers claim divine sanction or a sacred role to justify their authority and command loyalty. It can take the form of divine kingship, a caliphal title or a ruler's link to sacred institutions.

religious-persecution-and-sectarian-stri.s: Religious persecution and sectarian strife are a recurring cause of imperial weakness, as conflict between faiths or within a faith alienates subjects and divides elites. Rulers who impose religious uniformity may provoke revolt or lose productive communities.

religious-pluralism.s: Religious pluralism is the coexistence of several religions within a single society or state. The Khazar Khaganate was notable for accommodating Judaism, Christianity, Islam and traditional beliefs, which eased commercial relations with diverse partners.

religious-tolerance.s: Religious tolerance is the acceptance by a state of religious beliefs and practices different from those of its rulers. The Achaemenid Empire under Cyrus the Great allowed deported peoples to return and rebuild their temples, as recorded on the Cyrus Cylinder.

renaissance.s: The Renaissance was a period of cultural revival in Europe from the fourteenth to the sixteenth century, beginning in Italy and centred on the recovery of classical learning. It drew on Greek texts and scholars from the Byzantine Empire, on Arabic science from the Abbasid…

renaissance-of-the-12th-century.s: The Renaissance of the 12th century was a period of intellectual revival in western Europe marked by the recovery of Greek and Arabic learning, the growth of cathedral schools and the rise of the first universities. It built on the classical Latin texts preserved and copied…

repatriation-of-cultural-property.s: Repatriation of cultural property refers to the return of artworks and artefacts removed from their countries or communities of origin, often through conquest or colonial looting. The Benin Bronzes, some 3,000 works taken by British forces from the Benin Empire in 1897, are…

republic-of-turkey.s: The Republic of Turkey is the modern state founded in Anatolia after the dissolution of the Ottoman Empire following the First World War. Established under the leadership of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, it replaced the sultanate and caliphate with a secular, nationalist republic…

republican-party-brazil.s: The Republican Party of Brazil was a political movement founded in 1869 that campaigned for the replacement of the monarchy with a republic. Growing steadily through the 1880s, it attracted much of the landowning elite of São Paulo and offered an organised political…

republicanism.s: Republicanism refers to the political idea that the state should be a public matter governed by citizens or their representatives rather than by a hereditary monarch. It shaped the founding traditions of the Roman Republic that preceded the Roman Empire and resurfaced…

reservoir.s: A reservoir is an artificial or enlarged body of water used to store water for irrigation, drinking or flood control. In the Khmer Empire, vast reservoirs known as barays, together with canals and embankments, formed one of the most sophisticated hydraulic systems of the…

revolt-of-cyrus-the-younger.s: The Revolt of Cyrus the Younger was a rebellion in 401 BCE in which a Persian prince hired Greek mercenaries to seize the throne from his brother Artaxerxes II. Cyrus was killed at the Battle of Cunaxa, and the retreat of the surviving Greek force was recorded by Xenophon.

revolt-of-the-three-feudatories.s: The Revolt of the Three Feudatories was a rebellion in southern China between 1673 and 1681 led by powerful Chinese generals, among them Wu Sangui, who had been granted hereditary fiefdoms for helping the Qing conquest. When the Kangxi Emperor moved to abolish these fiefdoms,…

revolts-of-522-520-bce.s: The revolts of 522–520 BCE were a wave of rebellions that broke out across the Achaemenid Empire during the disputed succession that brought Darius I to the throne. Darius suppressed them in a series of campaigns later commemorated in the Behistun Inscription.

reza-abbasi.s: Reza Abbasi was a leading Persian painter and calligrapher active at the court of the Safavid ruler Shah Abbas I in Isfahan. He is celebrated for single-figure studies and graceful line drawings that influenced later Persian painting.

reza-qoli.s: Reza Qoli was the eldest son of Nader Shah, founder of the Afsharid Empire, and served for a time as a regent and commander. In 1741 Nader had him blinded on suspicion of involvement in a conspiracy against his life.

rhine.s: The Rhine is a major river of western Europe that flows from the Alps to the North Sea. Under the Carolingian Empire it served, with the Danube, as a principal commercial artery, and the Saxon Wars were fought against peoples living east of it.

rhinoplasty.s: Rhinoplasty is surgery to reconstruct or reshape the nose. Early descriptions of the procedure appear in the surgical compendium attributed to the Indian physician Sushruta.

rhodes.s: Rhodes is an island in the south-eastern Aegean Sea, off the coast of Anatolia, long valued as a naval and commercial base. In the seventh century it became a target of the first Arab fleets built under Muawiyah as governor of Syria.

ribat.s: A ribat was a fortified religious community or frontier stronghold in the Islamic world, combining military defence with devotion and study. The Almoravid movement grew from a ribat founded by the preacher Abd Allah ibn Yasin among the Lamtuna Berbers.

rice.s: Rice is a cereal grain cultivated in flooded paddies or dry fields and is a staple food across much of Asia and parts of West Africa. It underpinned the economies of many empires, including the Han, Song and Ming dynasties of China, the Khmer and Majapahit empires of Southeast…

rice-terrace.s: A rice terrace is a series of stepped, levelled fields cut into hillsides to allow the irrigated cultivation of rice on sloping ground. Terracing conserves water and soil and makes intensive farming possible in upland areas.

richard-i-of-england.s: Richard I of England, known as Richard the Lionheart, was King of England from 1189 to 1199 and a leading commander of the Third Crusade. He fought Saladin's forces in the Levant, taking part in the capture of Acre and winning victories on the coast, but did not retake Jerusalem.

ridda-wars.s: The Ridda Wars, or Wars of Apostasy, were a series of campaigns fought in 632–633 CE by the first caliph, Abu Bakr, against Arabian tribes that broke away after the death of the Prophet Muhammad. Many tribes rallied around rival prophetic claimants such as Musaylima and Sajah.

riksdag.s: The Riksdag is the national assembly of Sweden, whose origins lie in the late medieval and early modern period. During the era of the Swedish Empire it brought together representatives of the realm to approve taxation, levies and major decisions of state.

riksdag-of-the-estates.s: The Riksdag of the Estates was the form of the Swedish parliament in which representatives sat in four separate estates: the nobility, the clergy, the burghers and the peasantry. Its inclusion of a peasant estate was unusual among European assemblies of the time.

rim-sin-i.s: Rim-Sin I was a long-reigning king of Larsa in southern Mesopotamia and one of the most powerful rulers of the region in the early second millennium BCE. A contemporary letter quoted in the Babylonian Empire profile names him alongside Hammurabi as one of several kings of…

rim-sin-ii.s: Rim-Sin II was a pretender who led a widespread rebellion of southern Mesopotamian cities against Babylon shortly after the death of Hammurabi. According to the Babylonian Empire profile, the revolt spread across 26 southern cities and was crushed by Hammurabi's son Samsu-iluna.

rimush.s: Rimush was a king of the Akkadian Empire and a son and successor of Sargon of Akkad. His reign was dominated by campaigns to suppress revolts among the Sumerian cities and other subject territories.

ringstrasse.s: The Ringstrasse is a grand circular boulevard in Vienna built in the second half of the nineteenth century on the site of the demolished city walls. It was lined with major public buildings, including parliament, the opera, museums and the university, as well as private…

rinji.s: Rinji was the Hausa term for slave villages or plantation settlements attached to the estates of emirs, officials and wealthy merchants in the Sokoto Caliphate. Enslaved people living in them produced grain and other crops for their owners.

rio-de-janeiro.s: Rio de Janeiro is a major port city on the south-eastern coast of Brazil. It became the seat of the Portuguese court in 1808 and then served as the capital of the Brazilian Empire throughout its existence.

rio-de-la-plata.s: The Río de la Plata is the broad estuary formed by the Paraná and Uruguay rivers on the border of modern Argentina and Uruguay, and by extension the surrounding region. Control of its eastern bank was contested between Portuguese Brazil and Spanish, later Argentine, authorities.

rio-grande-do-sul.s: Rio Grande do Sul is the southernmost province, now a state, of Brazil, bordering Uruguay and Argentina. During the Brazilian Empire it was the scene of the Farroupilha or Ragamuffin War of 1835–1845, in which republican separatists maintained an independent republic for…

roads-and-communication-networks.s: Roads and communication networks refers to the recurring pattern in which empires built routes, relay stations and postal systems to move armies, officials, information and goods across large territories. Such networks allowed central governments to collect taxes, respond to…

robert-sherley.s: Robert Sherley was an English adventurer who, with his brother Anthony, travelled to the court of the Safavid ruler Shah Abbas I at the end of the sixteenth century. He later served the shah as an envoy to European courts.

rock-hewn-churches-of-lalibela.s: The rock-hewn churches of Lalibela are a group of medieval churches carved directly out of rock in the town of Lalibela in the highlands of northern Ethiopia. They are traditionally associated with King Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty and are a major site of Ethiopian Orthodox…

rokosz.s: Rokosz was the legally recognised right of the Polish nobility to form a confederation in armed rebellion against a king believed to have violated his obligations. It was grounded in the conditions the nobility imposed on elected monarchs, including the Henrician Articles of…

roman-annexation-of-egypt.s: The Roman annexation of Egypt took place in 30 BCE, when Octavian took Alexandria after the defeat of Mark Antony and Cleopatra VII. Following the deaths of Antony and Cleopatra, Egypt became a Roman province under the direct control of the emperor.

roman-annexation-of-syria.s: The Roman annexation of Syria took place in 63 BCE, when the Roman general Pompey deposed the last Seleucid rulers and organised Syria as a Roman province. By then the Seleucid state had been reduced to a small, divided remnant around Antioch.

roman-empire.s: The Roman Empire was the state ruled by emperors from Rome after the end of the Roman Republic, at its height controlling the entire Mediterranean world and much of western Europe and the Near East. Its western half ended with the deposition of Romulus Augustulus in 476 CE,…

roman-expedition-against-the-garamantes-.n: Roman expedition against the Garamantes (19 BCE)
roman-expedition-against-the-garamantes-.s: The Roman expedition against the Garamantes was a punitive campaign led in 19 BCE by Lucius Cornelius Balbus, the proconsul of Africa, into the Fezzan region of the central Sahara. According to the Garamantian Empire profile, Balbus captured fifteen Garamantian settlements,…

roman-law.s: Roman law is the legal system developed in ancient Rome from the Twelve Tables through centuries of statutes, magistrates' edicts and the writings of jurists. It was systematised in the sixth century under the Byzantine emperor Justinian in the Corpus Juris Civilis.

roman-republic.s: The Roman Republic was the system of government of ancient Rome from the expulsion of the kings, traditionally dated to 509 BCE, until the rise of Augustus in the late first century BCE. Governed by elected magistrates and the Senate, it expanded across Italy and the…

roman-senate.s: The Roman Senate was the governing council of ancient Rome, composed largely of former magistrates and members of leading families. Under the Roman Republic it directed foreign policy, finance and war, while under the emperors its authority became largely formal.

roman-triumph.s: The Roman triumph was a ceremonial procession through Rome granted to a victorious general, in which he paraded with his troops, captives and spoils. Under the emperors the honour was increasingly reserved for members of the imperial family.

romania.s: Romania is a country in south-eastern Europe, formed in the nineteenth century from the union of the principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia. After the First World War it was greatly enlarged with territories, including Transylvania, taken from the dissolved Austro-Hungarian…

romanians.s: Romanians are a people of south-eastern Europe who speak a Romance language derived from Latin. Within the Austro-Hungarian Empire, large Romanian communities lived in Transylvania and other eastern regions under Hungarian administration.

romanos-iv-diogenes.s: Romanos IV Diogenes was a Byzantine emperor who reigned from 1068 to 1071. He led a major campaign against the Seljuk Turks and was defeated and captured by Sultan Alp Arslan at the Battle of Manzikert in 1071.

romanticism.s: Romanticism was a cultural and intellectual movement of the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries that emphasised emotion, imagination, the past and national identity. In Poland it was closely bound up with the loss of statehood after the partitions.

romanus-pontifex.s: Romanus Pontifex is a papal bull, one of a series of fifteenth-century papal documents that granted Iberian crowns rights over newly encountered lands and peoples outside Christendom. The Spanish Empire profile cites it, together with Inter Caetera and the Treaty of…

rome.s: Rome is a city in central Italy that grew from a small settlement on the Tiber into the capital of the Roman Republic and Roman Empire, and later the seat of the papacy. As the centre of Roman power it fought Carthage, conquered the Seleucid, Ptolemaic and Macedonian kingdoms…

romulus-augustulus.s: Romulus Augustulus was the last emperor of the Western Roman Empire, a youth placed on the throne by his father, the general Orestes. He was deposed in 476 CE by the Germanic commander Odoacer, a date conventionally used to mark the end of Roman rule in the West.

rostam-farrokhzad.s: Rostam Farrokhzad was a Sasanian Persian general and leading figure at the court in the final years of the Sasanian Empire. He commanded the Persian army at the Battle of al-Qadisiyyah, where he was defeated and killed by Arab Muslim forces under Saad ibn Abi Waqqas.

round-city-of-baghdad.s: The Round City of Baghdad, officially named Madinat al-Salam or the City of Peace, was the circular walled capital founded in 762 by the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur on the Tigris. Its concentric walls enclosed the caliphal palace and great mosque at the centre, with gates facing…

rouran-khaganate.s: The Rouran Khaganate was a nomadic confederation that dominated the Mongolian steppe from the late fourth to the mid-sixth century CE. The Göktürks under Bumin of the Ashina clan were originally its vassals, and their revolt destroyed Rouran power in the 550s.

royal-navy.s: The Royal Navy is the naval service of Britain, which developed from the English navy into the most powerful fleet in the world between the eighteenth and early twentieth centuries. It protected trade routes, defended the British Isles and projected power to colonies across…

royal-niger-company.s: The Royal Niger Company was a British chartered company that held a commercial monopoly and administrative powers over territories along the lower Niger in the 1880s and 1890s. Its charter was revoked in 1900, when its territories passed to the British government and became…

royal-road.s: The Royal Road was an ancient highway of the Achaemenid Empire running about 2,700 kilometres from Susa to Sardis, with relay stations along its length. Royal couriers using fresh horses could carry messages across it in around seven days.

rozvi-empire.s: The Rozvi Empire was a state on the Zimbabwean plateau that emerged in the late seventeenth century under the Changamire dynasty, after breaking away from and overshadowing the Mutapa state. Its economy rested on cattle-based patronage, the gold and ivory trade and tribute…

rubattino-shipping-company.s: The Rubattino shipping company was a Genoese steamship company that purchased land at Assab Bay on the Red Sea coast in 1869. In 1882 the Italian government assumed control of the site.

rubber.s: Rubber is an elastic material produced from the latex of certain tropical trees, which became an important industrial commodity in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries with the growth of bicycles, automobiles and electrical industries. Colonial powers established…

rule-of-law.s: The rule of law is the principle that all people and institutions, including governments, are subject to and accountable under publicly known laws applied equally. It is closely associated with British constitutional traditions.

rupee.s: The rupee is a currency unit of the Indian subcontinent, descended from the silver rupiya coin introduced in the sixteenth century and later standardised under Mughal rule. It remained the main unit of account in South Asia into the colonial and modern periods.

rupiya.s: The rupiya was a silver coin introduced in northern India in the sixteenth century under Sher Shah Suri and adopted as the standard silver coinage of the Mughal Empire. Its consistent weight and purity made it widely trusted in trade.

russia.s: Russia is a vast country spanning eastern Europe and northern Asia, which grew from the principality of Moscow into the Russian Empire and later the Soviet Union. As a major power it fought repeatedly against the Swedish Empire, the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and the…

russian-empire.s: The Russian Empire was the state ruled by the Romanov dynasty from Peter the Great's proclamation of the empire in 1721 until the revolution of 1917. It expanded across eastern Europe, the Caucasus, Central Asia and Siberia to become one of the largest empires in history.

russian-judicial-reform-of-1864.s: The Russian judicial reform of 1864 was one of the Great Reforms of Tsar Alexander II, which reorganised the courts of the Russian Empire. It introduced public trials, trial by jury for serious criminal cases, independent judges, an organised legal profession and justices of…

russian-orthodox-church.s: The Russian Orthodox Church is the branch of Eastern Orthodox Christianity that developed after the conversion of Kievan Rus in the late tenth century. It became closely tied to Muscovite and then Russian imperial authority, and Peter the Great placed it under state control by…

russian-revolution-of-1905.s: The Russian Revolution of 1905 was a wave of strikes, peasant uprisings, mutinies and political protest across the Russian Empire, sparked by the Bloody Sunday massacre in Saint Petersburg and defeat in the war with Japan. It forced Tsar Nicholas II to issue the October…

russo-japanese-war.s: The Russo-Japanese War was a conflict between the Russian Empire and the Empire of Japan over influence in Manchuria and Korea, concluded by the Treaty of Portsmouth in 1905. Japan won decisive victories on land and at sea, including the destruction of the Russian fleet at…

russo-turkish-war-1768-1774.s: The Russo-Turkish War of 1768–1774 was a conflict between the Russian Empire under Catherine the Great and the Ottoman Empire. Russian forces won major victories on land and at sea, and the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca ended the war by granting Russia access to the Black Sea and…

russo-turkish-war-1877-1878.s: The Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878 was fought between the Russian Empire and the Ottoman Empire, following uprisings among the Balkan Christian peoples. Russia's victory led to the Treaty of San Stefano and then the Congress of Berlin in 1878, which recognised the independence…

rye.s: Rye is a hardy cereal grain that grows well in cool climates and poorer soils, long a staple of northern and eastern European agriculture. The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth exported large quantities of rye and wheat through the Baltic port of Gdańsk to the Netherlands,…
